concept.name: Availability heuristic
concept.definition: A mental shortcut, identified by Tversky and Kahneman (1973), in which the judged frequency or probability of an event depends on how easily instances come to mind rather than on actual base rates. Ease of recall - driven by recency, vividness, emotion, and media exposure - substitutes for statistical reasoning.
concept.intuition: If you can picture it quickly, you think it is common; after a week of crash headlines, a crash feels imminent.
concept.mechanics: Frequency judgments are made from the number or experienced ease of retrieved examples, as in the classic 'words starting with K' experiment; Schwarz and colleagues showed the felt ease of retrieval itself carries the effect. In markets, vivid recent events such as crashes or hot IPOs are overweighted relative to their base rates.
concept.failure_modes: It misleads exactly where media coverage or personal experience is unrepresentative - vivid but rare risks are overweighted while common, dull ones are ignored. Later critiques note ambiguity in whether ease or content of recall drives the effect, complicating measurement.
concept.misconceptions: Availability is not simple recency; vividness, emotion, and repetition also drive it. Nor is the heuristic always wrong - availability often correlates with true frequency, which is why it persists; the bias lies in its systematic distortions.
concept.example: After weeks of coverage of a crypto collapse, a trader overestimates the probability of an imminent broad-market crash and buys expensive hedges, though long-run base rates are unchanged.
